Find the statement that is false.
(B) True — the lanthanoids are strongly electropositive, so their +3 compounds are largely ionic.
(C) True — this is the lanthanoid contraction. The 4f electrons shield the nucleus poorly, so the
effective nuclear charge rises steadily and the ionic radius falls from La³⁺ to Lu³⁺.
(D) True — Ln(OH)₃ are basic, though they grow slightly less so across the series as the ion shrinks.
(A) False — most Ln(III) ions are coloured, because an electron can be promoted between 4f
orbitals and those f–f transitions absorb visible light. Nd³⁺ is pink, Pr³⁺ green, Er³⁺ rose.
Only the ones with an empty, half-filled or full 4f shell are colourless: La³⁺ (4f⁰), Gd³⁺ (4f⁷)
and Lu³⁺ (4f¹⁴), because no f–f transition is available to them.
∴ statement (A) is wrong.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|41||0|0:
A square planar complex has its four ligands at the corners of a square, so each ligand has
one partner directly opposite it (trans) and two beside it (cis).
With four *different* unidentate ligands A, B, X and L, fix A at one corner.
The isomer is then completely decided by which of the other three sits opposite A:
1. A trans to B (so X and L are cis to A)
2. A trans to X (so B and L are cis to A)
3. A trans to L (so B and X are cis to A)
There are three geometrical isomers, and no more — rotating the square does not create new ones.
In each one, relative to A, two ligands are cis and one is trans.
Note this is unlike a tetrahedral MABXL, which shows no geometrical isomerism at all because
every position is adjacent to every other.
∴ two cis and one trans.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|42||0|0:
Crystal field theory treats the metal–ligand interaction as purely electrostatic.
The metal is taken as a bare positive ion and each ligand as a point negative charge, or as the
negative end of a dipole. No sharing of electrons is allowed for.
The whole of the theory follows from that assumption: the ligand point charges repel the metal's
d electrons, and because the five d orbitals point in different directions they are repelled by
different amounts. That is what splits them into t₂g and e₉ and gives Δ₀.
The assumption is what makes the theory simple, and also what makes it incomplete — it cannot
explain the spectrochemical series, where neutral CO outranks the charged F⁻.
That required ligand field and molecular orbital theory, which do allow covalent overlap.
∴ according to crystal field theory the M–L bond is purely ionic.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|43||0|0.s:
Coordination number counts donor atoms, not ligands.
en (ethane-1,2-diamine) is bidentate — it donates through both nitrogens. Two of them give 2 × 2 = 4.
Oxalate, C₂O₄²⁻, is also bidentate — two oxygens. That gives 2 more.
Coordination number = 4 + 2 = 6.
Now the oxidation state. NO₂⁻ lies outside the square brackets, so it is the counter ion and the
complex ion must be +1 to balance it.
Inside: en is neutral (0 each), oxalate carries 2−.
x + 2(0) + (−2) = +1
x − 2 = +1 ⇒ x = +3
∴ 6 and 3.

kcet|Chemistry|2017|44||0|0:
The ring is the electron-rich partner here, so it is attacked by an electrophile.
FeCl₃ is a Lewis acid; it polarises the halogen and generates the electrophile:
Cl₂ + FeCl₃ ⇒ Cl⁺ + [FeCl₄]⁻
The π cloud of the ring attacks Cl⁺ to give an arenium ion, and then a proton is lost to restore
aromaticity. A hydrogen has been replaced by chlorine — substitution, not addition.
The ring keeps its aromatic sextet throughout, which is why benzene rings substitute rather than add.
The –CH₃ of toluene is electron releasing by inductive and hyperconjugative effects, and it
stabilises the intermediate most when the attack is at the ortho and para positions — hence those products.
(C) free radical conditions (UV light, no FeCl₃) would attack the side chain instead, giving C₆H₅CH₂Cl.
∴ electrophilic substitution.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|45||0|0:
Follow it one reagent at a time.
CH₃Br + KCN — cyanide is a strong nucleophile and displaces bromide (SN2):
A = CH₃CN, methyl cyanide (acetonitrile). One carbon has been added to the chain.
A + H₃O⁺ — acid hydrolysis of a nitrile goes through the amide to the acid:
B = CH₃COOH, ethanoic acid.
B + LiAlH₄ — lithium aluminium hydride is strong enough to reduce a carboxylic acid all the way
to the primary alcohol (NaBH₄ would not touch it):
C = CH₃CH₂OH, ethanol.
Keep count of the carbons: 1 in CH₃Br, 2 after the cyanide step, and 2 at the end ✓
∴ C is ethyl alcohol.
kcet|Chemistry|2017|46||0|0:
Acidity of a phenol is set by how well the ring stabilises the phenoxide ion left behind.
An electron-withdrawing group pulls charge away from the O⁻ and stabilises it ⇒ more acidic.
An electron-releasing group pushes charge onto it and destabilises it ⇒ less acidic.
o-Cresol has a –CH₃ group, which releases electrons by induction and hyperconjugation.
Its phenoxide is less stable than phenol's, so o-cresol is the weakest acid of the three.
o-Nitrophenol has –NO₂, strongly electron withdrawing by both −I and −R. It delocalises the
negative charge onto the nitro oxygens, so its anion is much the most stable and it is the strongest acid.
Putting them in order of increasing acidity:
o-cresol < phenol < o-nitrophenol
∴ option (B).

kcet|Chemistry|2017|47||0|0.s:
To stop at the aldehyde the oxidation must not be allowed to continue, and the usual way to
ensure that is to keep water out — water lets the aldehyde form a hydrate, which is oxidised on
to the acid.
(A) CrO₃ in an anhydrous medium — no water, so it stops at RCHO ✓
(C) PCC is Cr(VI) in dichloromethane, again non-aqueous ✓
(D) Heating the vapour over copper at 573 K is a catalytic dehydrogenation, giving RCHO + H₂ ✓
(B) KMnO₄ in acidic medium is a powerful oxidant in an aqueous medium. The aldehyde formed
is oxidised immediately, and the product isolated is the carboxylic acid RCOOH, not RCHO.
∴ acidified KMnO₄ cannot be used.
